posts.title: How to install AppDrop
posts.excerpt: The best store for downloading apps on your jailbroken iOS device.
posts.content:
Welcome to the first blog post on this page.
Today, I’ll show you how to install AppDrop—the best store for those with a jailbroken Apple device.

So, let’s get started.
Open Cydia or Zebra, go to Sources, and tap the "+" icon.
Enter the following source URL: https://adrienrl1.github.io/cydia/

Note: If you are using a much older version of iOS, use http://adrienrl1.github.io/cydia/ instead.

Once that’s done, tap on the "AdrienRL" source, go to "All Packages," and then select "AppDrop."
Tap "Modify" > "Install."

After the installation is complete, the app will appear on your home screen.

OPENING THE APP:
When you open the app, you’ll be greeted by a home screen containing various folders filled with applications.

It uses archive.org to retrieve the .ipa files.

Make sure you have Filza File Manager installed so you can view the downloaded IPA files.

Thanks for reading, and see you in the next post!

posts.title: Rooting Android and Its Consequences: Should I Really Root My Old Device?
posts.excerpt: Thinking about rooting your old Android phone? Explore the benefits, risks, security concerns and everything you should consider before taking control of your device.
posts.content:
# Rooting Android and Its Consequences: Should I Really Root My Old Device?

**Android has always been known for its flexibility.** Unlike many other mobile operating systems, it gives users a considerable amount of control over how their devices look and behave. But there is one subject that has remained part of the Android community for years: rooting.

For some people, rooting is the best way to get more out of an older smartphone. For others, it is an unnecessary risk that can turn a perfectly usable device into a frustrating experience.

So, is rooting still worth it, especially if you have an older Android device sitting around?

Let's take a closer look.

## What exactly is rooting?

Android is built on Linux, and like other Linux-based systems, it uses different permission levels to control what users and applications can access.

Normally, Android users operate without full administrative privileges. This is intentional. It helps protect important system components and prevents applications from making changes that could affect the entire device.

Root access removes many of those restrictions by giving the user administrator-level permissions.

In simple terms, rooting gives you much deeper control over Android. You can access areas of the system that are normally restricted, use certain advanced applications and make modifications that would otherwise be impossible.

However, having more control also means having more responsibility.

## Why do people root their Android devices?

There was a time when rooting was almost a hobby for Android enthusiasts. Online communities were full of people experimenting with custom ROMs, kernels, themes and modifications.

One of the biggest reasons was customization. Users wanted to change things that manufacturers did not allow them to modify, from system behavior to visual elements.

Another reason was software support. Many older smartphones stopped receiving official Android updates long before their hardware became completely unusable. Custom ROMs offered another possibility, allowing some devices to run newer versions of Android through community-developed software.

There were also applications that required root access to perform advanced tasks, such as managing certain system settings or creating complete device backups.

For someone who enjoys experimenting with technology, it is easy to understand the appeal.

## The advantages of rooting an old device

Rooting can make an older Android phone more interesting to use, particularly if you enjoy exploring how the operating system works.

Some of the potential benefits include:

**More control over the system.** Root access allows advanced modifications that are unavailable on a standard Android installation.

**Greater customization.** Certain tools can change system behavior and provide additional options for experienced users.

**Custom ROM compatibility.** Depending on the device and its developer community, alternative Android distributions may offer a different experience or extend software support.

**Access to advanced applications.** Some utilities offer additional functionality when root permissions are available.

Still, these benefits depend heavily on the exact device, its Android version and the quality of the available community support.

Rooting does not magically improve a phone's processor, increase its physical memory or repair an aging battery. It simply gives you more freedom to modify the software.

## The consequences nobody should ignore

This is where things become more complicated.

Rooting is not a harmless customization option. Depending on how it is performed and how the device is configured afterward, it can introduce several problems.

**Security is one of the biggest concerns.**

Android's permission system exists for a reason. When an application receives root access, it may gain the ability to make changes far beyond what an ordinary application can do. Giving those permissions to an untrusted application can put personal information and the entire system at risk.

There is also the possibility of losing access to certain services. Some banking applications, games and streaming platforms check whether a device meets their security requirements. A rooted device may fail those checks, even if everything appears to work normally.

Updates can become another issue. Official system updates may no longer install as expected, particularly when system components have been modified. Some devices also have manufacturer-specific restrictions that complicate the process.

And then there is the possibility of making the device unusable. Incorrect modifications can prevent Android from starting properly. Recovery may be possible, but it is not guaranteed, and some situations require specialized repair.

Warranty coverage is another consideration. The consequences vary by manufacturer and local consumer protection laws, so it is worth checking the applicable terms before making changes.

## Is rooting worth it in 2026?

The answer depends on what you want to achieve.

If you have an old Android phone that you no longer use as your primary device, rooting might be an interesting project. It can be a way to learn more about Android, explore alternative software and understand how mobile operating systems work.

However, if the device is still your everyday phone, the decision deserves much more consideration.

Losing access to banking services, encountering update problems or weakening the device's security can easily outweigh the benefits of having additional customization options.

It is also important to remember that rooting is not the only way to improve an older Android experience. Removing unnecessary applications, freeing up storage, keeping applications updated and using lighter alternatives can already make a difference without changing the system's security model.

## Before making your decision

There are a few things worth considering before modifying an older device:

- Check whether your exact model has reliable community support.
- Understand the security implications of granting root permissions.
- Consider whether you actually need the features that root provides.
- Make sure you understand the recovery options available for your device.
- Think about whether you depend on applications that may reject rooted devices.

Most importantly, do not root a device just because someone online claims it will make Android faster. That is not what root access is designed to do.

## Final thoughts

Rooting remains one of the most interesting parts of Android's history and identity. It represents something that has always attracted enthusiasts to the platform: the ability to experiment, customize and take control of their own devices.

But the Android world has changed. Security requirements have become stricter, applications increasingly rely on device integrity checks, and manufacturers have introduced more restrictions.

For an old smartphone used as a secondary device or a personal technology project, rooting can still be worth exploring. For a phone that contains your everyday data and handles important tasks, staying with the original software may be the smarter choice.

**The real question is not whether you can root your Android device. It is whether you actually need to.**

posts.title: Why Is Windows 7 Simply the Best Operating System Microsoft Has Ever Made?
posts.excerpt: From the troubled Longhorn project and the early Windows 7 builds to its impact on the PC market, we explore why Windows 7 became a classic — and whether it still makes sense to use in 2027.
posts.content:
# Why Is Windows 7 Simply the Best Operating System Microsoft Has Ever Made?

*From the troubled Longhorn project to the golden age of desktop computing, discover how Windows 7 became one of Microsoft's most recognizable operating systems — and whether it still deserves a place on your PC in 2027.*

There is something special about Windows 7. For millions of people, it was more than an operating system: it was the desktop they grew up with, the place where they played their first PC games, discovered new software, customized their wallpapers and learned what a personal computer could do.

Its glass-like windows, familiar Start menu and redesigned taskbar gave it an identity that was instantly recognizable. But Windows 7 did not appear out of nowhere. Its story begins with a project that became one of Microsoft's most complicated development efforts: Windows Longhorn.

So how did Microsoft go from Longhorn's ambitious plans to one of its most beloved releases? And is Windows 7 still a sensible choice in 2027? Let's take a closer look.

## 1. The Longhorn project: ambition turns into trouble

After Windows XP, Microsoft began working on the next major version of Windows under the codename Longhorn. The project was expected to bring significant changes to the operating system, including a new storage technology called WinFS, a redesigned presentation and application framework known as Avalon, and a new communications infrastructure called Indigo.

Early Longhorn builds attracted considerable attention. They showed experimental interfaces, new visual effects and ideas that seemed to point toward a very different future for Windows.

However, the project grew increasingly complicated. Features were added, development became difficult to coordinate, and the original schedule slipped. At the same time, Microsoft was facing growing pressure to improve the security and reliability of Windows XP.

In 2004, Microsoft made a major decision: it would reset Longhorn development and rebuild the project on a more manageable foundation. Much of the planned technology was delayed, redesigned or abandoned. The work that continued eventually became Windows Vista.

Calling Longhorn simply a failure would miss an important part of the story. It was an ambitious project whose scope became difficult to deliver. Some of its ideas influenced later Windows releases, while others never became part of a finished product.

The reset also taught Microsoft a valuable lesson: a new operating system needed more than impressive features. It needed a stable foundation and a development process that could deliver them.

## 2. From Vista to Windows 7

Windows Vista launched in 2007 with a major visual redesign, new security features and the Aero interface. It also faced criticism over performance on some hardware, driver compatibility, software support and the User Account Control experience.

Vista was not universally bad, and many of its technologies became the foundation for the Windows that followed. But its reputation created a difficult situation for Microsoft.

The next release, developed under the codename Windows 7, took a more focused approach. Rather than replacing the entire platform again, Microsoft refined the technology introduced with Vista, worked on performance and compatibility, and improved the details of everyday use.

That distinction matters. Windows 7 was built on Vista's technical foundation, but it was not merely a cosmetic update. Microsoft made substantial changes to the user experience, system behavior, device support and the way common tasks were handled.

The goal was not to make Windows look completely unfamiliar. It was to make the existing experience feel more polished and dependable.

## 3. The beta days: watching Windows 7 take shape

The development period was especially exciting for Windows enthusiasts because Microsoft made important pre-release versions available to the public.

At the Professional Developers Conference in October 2008, Microsoft demonstrated an early Windows 7 pre-beta build, commonly associated with build 6801. It offered an early look at the direction of the new operating system.

In January 2009, the public Beta, build 7000, gave a much wider audience the chance to try Windows 7. People could explore the redesigned taskbar, test applications, check hardware compatibility and see how the system performed on their own computers.

The Release Candidate followed in May 2009. By then, Windows 7 was much closer to its final form, and the public testing period had helped build considerable anticipation.

Windows 7 reached Release to Manufacturing on July 22, 2009. The retail launch followed on October 22, 2009.

For enthusiasts, those beta and RC releases were a memorable part of the story. They made the development of a major Windows release feel like something users could follow and experience, rather than something hidden entirely behind Microsoft's doors.

## 4. Aero Glass: a desktop with its own identity

One of the first things people remember about Windows 7 is its appearance.

Aero Glass used translucent window borders, subtle reflections, smooth animations and carefully designed visual effects. The result was a desktop that felt distinctive without making the interface difficult to understand.

The visual experience was supported by practical features. Aero Peek made it possible to preview the desktop or inspect open windows. Aero Snap made arranging windows easier by letting users move them to the edges of the screen. Aero Shake offered a quick way to minimize other windows.

Personalization also played an important role. Users could choose wallpapers, window colors, sounds and themes, making the desktop feel like their own space.

Then there was the taskbar.

Windows 7 introduced a redesigned taskbar often called the Superbar. Pinned applications, clearer window grouping, thumbnail previews and Jump Lists made it easier to launch programs and return to recent files or common tasks.

These features were not revolutionary individually. Their strength was how naturally they worked together. Windows 7 made the desktop feel polished, useful and recognizable.

## 5. More than a pretty interface

Windows 7's reputation was not built on Aero alone.

Microsoft worked on responsiveness, memory management, startup behavior, device support and compatibility. The experience varied depending on the computer, but many users found Windows 7 more comfortable and responsive than Vista on comparable hardware.

The operating system also benefited from a broad software and hardware ecosystem. Many applications and devices designed for Windows XP or Vista continued to work, helping home users and organizations make the transition.

Some of the features that became part of everyday Windows 7 use included:

- Libraries for bringing files from different locations together.
- Improved taskbar previews and Jump Lists.
- HomeGroup for simpler home-network sharing.
- Better window management with Aero Snap and Aero Peek.
- Improved Windows Search.
- Device Stage for supported hardware.
- Broad support for 64-bit computing and modern PC hardware of its time.

Windows 7 did not ask users to relearn everything. It improved familiar parts of Windows while adding useful shortcuts and refinements.

That balance was one of its greatest strengths.

## 6. Its importance in the PC market

Windows 7 arrived at a critical moment for Microsoft.

Vista had struggled to win over some consumers and businesses, and many organizations were still using Windows XP. Microsoft needed a release that could restore confidence and provide a practical upgrade path.

Windows 7 became a major commercial success. In January 2010, Microsoft announced that it had sold more than 60 million Windows 7 licenses, describing it as the fastest-selling operating system in its history at the time.

It spread across home desktops, laptops, office computers, schools and gaming machines. For many manufacturers, it became the standard Windows experience on a new generation of PCs.

Its success also helped move businesses away from Windows XP. That transition took years, but Windows 7 became an important step in the evolution of the Windows PC ecosystem.

The operating system's influence was not limited to sales. Its taskbar design, window-management features and overall visual identity helped define what many people expected from a desktop operating system.

Windows 7 became a reference point — a version people would compare later releases against.

## 7. Why does Windows 7 still have so many fans?

There is no single reason.

For some users, it is the Aero interface: the glass effects, the colors, the wallpapers and the feeling of a carefully designed desktop. For others, it is the familiar Start menu, the straightforward control panels or the way the taskbar behaves.

There is also the software and gaming history attached to it. Many programs, games and peripherals from the late 2000s and early 2010s were designed with Windows 7 in mind. On suitable hardware, returning to that environment can feel like revisiting a particular moment in PC history.

Nostalgia is part of the appeal, but it is not the whole explanation. Windows 7 was widely adopted, commercially successful and genuinely useful for a broad range of computers.

It had flaws, of course. No operating system is perfect. But its combination of familiarity, customization, compatibility and visual design gave it a lasting reputation.

## 8. Should you still use Windows 7 in 2027?

This is the question that deserves the most careful answer.

Windows 7 can still be useful for specific purposes: a retro PC, older software, period-correct gaming, hardware that lacks drivers for newer systems, or an offline computer dedicated to a particular task.

But there is a major difference between preserving an older operating system and depending on it for everyday online activities.

Microsoft ended regular support for Windows 7 on January 14, 2020. The Extended Security Updates program for eligible organizations ended in January 2023. Standard installations no longer receive regular security updates from Microsoft.

That creates real limitations. Newly discovered vulnerabilities may remain unpatched, modern browsers and applications may no longer support the system, and some websites or online services can become difficult to use.

For that reason, we do not recommend Windows 7 as the main operating system for a computer used for everyday internet browsing, banking, shopping or accounts containing important personal information.

If you want to enjoy Windows 7 in 2027, consider using it on a dedicated retro machine, keeping it offline where practical, and avoiding sensitive accounts. For daily online use, choose an operating system that still receives security updates.

Windows 7 can remain part of your setup without being responsible for everything.

## 9. The legacy of a Windows classic

The road to Windows 7 was not straightforward. Longhorn's ambitious plans ran into serious development problems, Vista had a difficult reception, and Microsoft had to rethink how it approached the next release.

The result was an operating system that brought together a stable technical foundation, a memorable interface and practical improvements that made everyday computing feel comfortable.

Windows 7 was not perfect, and it is no longer a safe choice for general-purpose online computing. But its place in PC history is secure.

It represented a moment when design and usability came together in a way that millions of people appreciated. It made the desktop feel personal, the taskbar genuinely useful and the overall experience cohesive.

**Windows 7 wasn't perfect. But for millions of people, it was exactly what an operating system was supposed to be.**
